market: Mobile, broadband, home insurance, mortgages, cash savings
title: Tackling the loyalty penalty: response to a super-complaint made by Citizens Advice
method: Review of existing estimates and evidence across five essential markets, in response to the Citizens Advice super-complaint
key_finding: Existing and loyal customers collectively pay a substantial loyalty penalty across five markets; the number affected ranges from under 1 million (mortgages) to over 12 million (home insurance)
reported_magnitude: around £4 billion in total per year across the 5 markets
caveats: Best estimates from available data with acknowledged evidence gaps; not a finding that overall prices are too high

market: Mobile, broadband, home insurance, mortgages, cash savings
title: Excessive prices for disengaged consumers: a super-complaint to the Competition and Markets Authority
data_period: research gathered 2017-2018 (incl. ComRes poll of 3,030 adults)
method: Nationally representative polling plus desk research and analysis of regulator and official data to estimate per-market penalties
key_finding: Disengaged and loyal consumers overpay across five markets; 8 in 10 bill-payers pay a penalty in at least one market
reported_magnitude: £4.1bn per annum in total; up to £877 more per year for a customer paying the penalty in all five markets
caveats: Citizens Advice states its analysis is not the final word; different assumptions yield different results; penalties are summed across markets

market: Mobile, broadband, home insurance, cash savings
title: Loyalty penalty update
method: Progress update two years on, combining published FCA and Ofcom estimates
key_finding: Combined FCA and Ofcom work found more than 28 million customers paying a loyalty penalty
reported_magnitude: £3.4 billion; more than 28 million customers
caveats: Combines separate FCA and Ofcom figures; customers in more than one market may be double-counted

title: General insurance pricing practices: final report (MS18/1.3)
method: Analysis of pricing data obtained from firms across the home and motor insurance markets
key_finding: Long-standing customers are price walked, paying more the longer they stay; new motor customers paid less than customers of five years or more
reported_magnitude: Motor: new customers £285 vs £370 for 5+ year customers; 6 million policyholders paid high prices in 2018 and would have saved £1.2bn at the average price for their risk
caveats: Figures are averages for a typical risk; the differential is not solely price walking, as risk and cost differences also apply

title: General insurance pricing practices: interim report (MS18/1.2)
method: Interim analysis of firm pricing data in the home and motor insurance markets
key_finding: Insurers discount for new customers then raise premiums at renewal (price walking), targeting increases at those less likely to switch
reported_magnitude: 6 million policyholders paid high prices in 2018; £1.2bn potential saving at the average price for their risk
caveats: Interim findings, later confirmed in the final report

title: General insurance pricing practices market study: policy statement (PS21/5)
method: Policy statement and cost-benefit analysis setting final pricing rules
key_finding: Introduced a pricing remedy requiring a renewal price no greater than the equivalent new-business price (ENBP) a firm would offer a new customer
reported_magnitude: £4.2bn consumer benefit reported in the FCA cost-benefit analysis (a consultants' alternative assumption gave £1.4bn)
caveats: Forward-looking estimate, sensitive to competition assumptions

title: Cash savings market study (MS14/2)
method: Analysis of provider balances and interest rates by account opening date
key_finding: Accounts opened longer ago pay lower interest; easy-access rates were higher on recently opened accounts than on accounts opened more than five years ago
reported_magnitude: Easy-access rates on average 0.82 percentage points higher on accounts opened in the last two years than on those opened more than five years ago (0.87 percentage points for cash ISAs)
caveats: Averages and aggregates based on June 2014 data

title: An evaluation of our general insurance pricing practices (GIPP) remedies (EP25/2)
method: Ex-post evaluation of the pricing remedies using firm data
key_finding: After the reforms the home-insurance premium gap between existing and new customers almost halved
reported_magnitude: Home existing-vs-new premium gap fell from £95.38 to £49.17 on average
caveats: Ex-post, against a backdrop of high insurance-price inflation; motor-market dynamics differ

title: Energy market investigation: final report
method: Direct estimate of detriment from excessive prices charged by the Six Large Energy Firms, cross-checked with cost benchmarking
key_finding: Around 70% of the Six Large Firms' customers were on default standard variable tariffs and overpaid relative to available tariffs
reported_magnitude: Detriment from excessive prices about £1.4 billion a year on average over 2012-2015, reaching almost £2 billion in 2015
caveats: CMA direct-approach estimate; relates specifically to the Six Large Energy Firms

title: Ofgem on course to cap poor value energy deals by end of 2018 (statement)
method: Policy statement supporting the introduction of the default tariff cap
key_finding: Around 12 million households on poor-value default deals overpaid relative to the cheapest tariffs; many had not switched for years
reported_magnitude: as much as £300 more than those on the cheapest tariffs; around 12 million households on default deals
caveats: The £300 figure is an illustrative maximum, not an average, and was stated before the cap level was set

title: Ofcom Annual Report and Accounts 2019/20 (reporting the September 2019 broadband pricing review)
method: Analysis of around 20 million customer tariffs comparing in-contract and out-of-contract broadband prices
key_finding: Around 8.8 million customers were out of contract and could save by re-contracting or switching, i.e. out-of-contract (loyal) customers pay more
reported_magnitude: around 8.8 million out of contract; savings up to £8 to £9 per month by re-contracting or up to £9 to £10 per month by switching
caveats: Expressed as maximum savings available (up to), not averages; figures as reported in Ofcom's annual report summarising its September 2019 review

organisation_or_authors: Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), reporting Ofcom analysis
title: Loyalty penalty update (reporting Ofcom's mobile analysis)
data_period: Ofcom review of the market in 2018 and 2019
method: CMA update summarising Ofcom analysis of customers who keep paying after a bundled handset and airtime contract's minimum term
key_finding: Of 2 million out-of-contract bundled customers, about 1.4 million would save by switching to a SIM-only deal (effectively still paying for a handset already paid off); the other 600,000 would pay more
reported_magnitude: around 1.4 million (of 2 million) would save an average of £11 a month; the remaining 600,000 would pay more (an average of £6 a month)
caveats: The £11 a month is the average saving available to those who would benefit, not a universal overpayment

title: Restoring electricity affordability and Australia's competitive advantage: Retail Electricity Pricing Inquiry, final report
method: Inquiry analysis of retailer data and documents, drawing on AEMC research on standing versus market offers
key_finding: Retailers do not reward loyalty but charge disengaged and loyal customers more via higher-priced standing offers (a loyalty tax)
reported_magnitude: gap between the median standing offer and the best market offer ranged from $273 (ACT) to $832 (South Australia) per year
caveats: The $273-$832 range is attributed by the ACCC to AEMC research; loyalty tax is a term the report notes others use; figures are Australian dollars

title: Home loan price inquiry: final report
method: Price inquiry using the RBA Securitisation Dataset; analysis of interest rates by loan age
key_finding: Existing borrowers pay higher interest rates than new borrowers, and the gap widens the longer a loan is held
reported_magnitude: on average about 58 basis points higher for loans 3-5 years old, 71 basis points for 5-10 years, and 104 basis points for loans over 10 years old, above the average rate for new loans
caveats: Averages as at September 2020 (1 basis point = 0.01%)

title: Competition in the Australian Financial System (Inquiry Report No. 89)
method: Public inquiry into competition in deposit accounts and mortgages, citing RBA data on existing versus new loan rates
key_finding: Loyal and existing customers get a worse deal; existing variable-rate home-loan customers pay more than new borrowers
reported_magnitude: variable rates for existing home-loan customers average about 0.3 to 0.4 percentage points higher than on new loans (an extra $66 to $87 per month on the average balance; paid by about 15% of existing customers)
caveats: The 0.3-0.4 percentage-point figure is reported by the Commission as sourced from the RBA; figures are Australian dollars

title: Review of differential pricing in the private car and home insurance markets: final report
method: Analysis of actual-premium-to-technical-premium ratios by customer tenure
key_finding: Through price walking, long-term customers (nine years or more with the same insurer) pay more than an equivalent first-time renewal customer
reported_magnitude: on average 14% more on private car insurance and 32% more on home insurance (tenure 9+ versus first renewal)
caveats: Averages relative to expected cost (technical premium); a ban on price walking followed, effective 1 July 2022

organisation_or_authors: EIOPA (European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority)
title: Supervisory statement on differential pricing practices in non-life insurance lines of business
method: Supervisory statement clarifying expectations under the Insurance Distribution Directive
key_finding: Repeated non-risk-based premium increases at renewal (price walking) unfairly penalise loyal customers, especially vulnerable groups
reported_magnitude: qualitative
caveats: Supervisory expectations only; no new empirical data or magnitude

market: Online e-commerce (TVs, airline tickets, hotels, sports shoes)
organisation_or_authors: European Commission (DG Justice and Consumers); study by Ipsos, London Economics and Deloitte
title: Consumer market study on online market segmentation through personalised pricing/offers in the European Union
data_period: mystery shopping in 8 EU Member States; 34,403 matched product pairs
method: Mystery-shopping experiment comparing personalisation versus no-personalisation scenarios across four markets
key_finding: Little evidence of consistent online personalised pricing; where price differences occurred they were rare and small (a contrary finding relative to the insurance loyalty penalty)
reported_magnitude: in 94% of 34,403 matched product pairs there was no price difference; in the remaining 6%, the median difference was less than 1.6%
caveats: Mystery-shopping method limitations; most differences were statistically insignificant and evenly distributed around zero; this is evidence against widespread online personalised pricing

title: Personalised pricing in the digital era: background note by the Secretariat
data_period: not stated (literature synthesis; cites a 2015 experiment)
method: Background note synthesising the literature, citing a laboratory and online experiment on personalised pricing
key_finding: In a cited experiment, sellers allowed to personalise prices charged a fixed fraction of each consumer's willingness to pay, not varying with the number of competing sellers
reported_magnitude: around 64% of willingness to pay across all experiments (cited experiment)
caveats: From a cited stylised experiment, not real-market data; a Secretariat background document

title: Surveillance pricing: a staff perspective (6(b) study initial findings)
method: Section 6(b) compulsory-process study of documents from six intermediary firms offering targeted-pricing and user-segmentation products
key_finding: Third-party intermediaries use a wide range of personal data (location, demographics, purchase, return and browsing history and real-time behaviour) to help retailers set individualised and targeted prices
reported_magnitude: qualitative
caveats: Initial, non-exhaustive staff findings based on only six respondents; no finding of illegal conduct; staff views, not necessarily the Commission's

title: Adverse selection and inertia in health insurance markets: when nudging hurts
data_period: not stated (six years of individual-level panel data from a large firm)
method: Natural experiment (forced active re-enrollment) with a structural discrete-choice model of plan choice
key_finding: Consumer inertia and switching costs in health-plan choice are large, and nudging consumers to switch can worsen adverse selection
reported_magnitude: estimated average family switching cost about $2,032 (population standard deviation $446); the nudge doubles the existing welfare loss from adverse selection
caveats: The $2,032 figure appears in the paper body (NBER working paper w17459); the published AER abstract reports that switching costs are large and the doubling result, not the dollar figure

market: General decision-making (incl. health plans, retirement programs)
title: Status quo bias in decision making
method: Decision-making experiments plus analysis of faculty health-plan and retirement-program selections
key_finding: Individuals disproportionately stick with the status quo, and the bias is substantial in important real decisions
reported_magnitude: qualitative
caveats: Foundational theoretical and experimental paper; no single headline magnitude

organisation_or_authors: Monica Giulietti, Catherine Waddams Price & Michael Waterson
title: Consumer choice and competition policy: a study of UK energy markets
method: Switching-decision model plus a survey of nearly 700 UK residential gas consumers
key_finding: Search and switching costs and limited switching left the incumbent supplier with considerable market power
reported_magnitude: qualitative (survey of nearly 700 consumers)
caveats: Conclusion on market power is qualitative; no single switching-rate figure in the abstract

organisation_or_authors: Chris M. Wilson & Catherine Waddams Price
title: Do consumers switch to the best supplier?
method: Empirical analysis of two consumer switching datasets, comparing realised with maximum available gains
key_finding: Consumers who switch capture only part of the available savings, and a sizeable share lose surplus by switching
reported_magnitude: price-motivated switchers appropriated only a quarter to half of the maximum gains available; 20-30% of consumers reduced their surplus by switching
caveats: Figures from the paper's abstract; switching does not reliably discipline the market
